theme: He trains my hands for war
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 18:31-50. The second half of David’s song moves from God’s character to David’s victories, and ends in praise among the nations.
settingTheScene: The first half of the psalm praised God as rescuer. The second half describes how God equips David for battle, gives him victory, and establishes his kingdom. It ends with a promise to praise God among the nations and a reference to “his anointed” and his offspring forever. This looks forward to the covenant you will read in 2 Samuel 7.
observation: “For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?” (v. 31).
“The God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless” (v. 32).
“He makes my feet like the feet of a deer and sets me secure on the heights” (v. 33).
“You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your gentleness made me great” (v. 35).
“You made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me” (v. 43).
“The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation” (v. 46).
“For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing to your name” (v. 49).
“Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever” (v. 50).
interpretation:
The second half of the psalm gives God credit for everything David has achieved. “The God who equipped me with strength.” “He trains my hands for war.” “You have given me the shield of your salvation.” David was a skilled warrior, but he does not say it. He says that God made him able. It is a model of how a believer should speak of any success.

One phrase stands out: “Your gentleness made me great.” The word is often translated “condescension” or “humility.” It is the picture of the great God bending down to raise a shepherd boy. David’s greatness is the result of God’s stooping. It is perhaps the most beautiful line in the psalm. God does not merely give power; he gives it with gentleness.

In verses 37 to 42, David describes his victories, in the strong language of ancient warfare. The point is not violence for its own sake, but the defeat of the enemies of God’s anointed. The nations that were hostile come to serve. David’s kingdom is established, and the psalm hints that it extends to people he had not known.

The ending is the most important part. David vows to praise God among the nations, a surprising foreshadowing of the mission of Israel to the world. And the last verse points beyond David: “Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.” The promise is for David’s descendants. This is what God will say in the covenant of 2 Samuel 7.

The psalm is a model of how to remember. It begins with love and ends with a promise. Everything in between is thanksgiving for what God has done.
connection: Paul quotes verse 49 in Romans 15:9 to show that the Messiah praises God among the Gentiles. Jesus is “David’s offspring forever,” the anointed who brings great salvation (Luke 1:32-33). Matthew 11:29 says that Jesus is “gentle and lowly in heart.” Philippians 2:5-11 shows him humbling himself and being exalted. Hebrews 2:13 puts words of Psalm 18 on Christ’s lips.
application:
When you succeed at something, practice saying, “God equipped me.”

Think about a time when God’s gentleness, not force, brought you through.

Pray for the nations to come to praise him.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for equipping and supporting you.
Thank him for his gentleness that makes you great.
Pray that his salvation would reach the nations.
